clue.text: That's surprising and it's sadly not something one could name

parts.note: the exclamation 'What!' expresses surprise

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Someone is startled and upset by a thing they cannot put a name to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's surprising' is the exclamation 'What!', not a comment on the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A whatsit is a placeholder word for an object whose proper name escapes the speaker.

clue.text: Wife, as a consequence, is from where?

parts.note: hence means therefore, as a result

explanation.surface: A question about where a wife comes from, prompted by some consequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Whence is an old-fashioned adverb asking from what place something comes.

clue.text: One university offered Dawn's song

parts.note: one is A, the indefinite article
bade is a past tense of bid, to offer

explanation.surface: A university gave a woman called Dawn a song to perform.
explanation.walkthrough: Dawn looks like a woman's name; read it as daybreak.
explanation.definitionFit: An aubade is a poem or piece of music celebrating or lamenting daybreak.

clue.text: Composer wants broadcaster to include trains (with volume adjusted)

indicators.note: the broadcaster's name is opened up to hold the other letters

parts.note: Sky is a British satellite TV broadcaster

indicators.note: adjusted means altered, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A composer asks a TV channel to feature trains, with the sound turned up or down.
explanation.walkthrough: Sky is a British satellite television company; the shuffled letters split it after its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Igor Stravinsky was the Russian-born composer of The Rite of Spring.

clue.text: Scatter, climbing over duke's house

indicators.note: the reversed scattering word goes over, that is around, the duke's letter
in a down clue, climbing means the word for scatter reads upwards, in reverse

parts.note: to rout an enemy is to scatter it in defeat
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: People scatter, clambering over a duke's stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' is not a building here but a royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tudors were the royal dynasty of England from Henry VII to Elizabeth I; a royal family is a house.

clue.text: Criminal rip-off in fashion

indicators.note: the letters go in the fashion word

parts.note: a cult is a fashionable craze

indicators.note: off means wrong or awry, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A criminal knock-off product is the latest trend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rip-off' looks like one word for a swindle; it splits into the fodder and its anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A culprit is the person guilty of an offence, the wrongdoer.

clue.text: So Eric frantically pulls in stomach when using one?

definitions.text: So Eric frantically pulls in stomach when using one?

indicators.note: the shuffled letters take in the stomach word
frantically suggests wild agitation, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
tum is informal for stomach

explanation.surface: Eric breathes in hard when visiting a costume maker to be fitted.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also hints at the definition: a costume supplier might make you pull your stomach in for a fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A costumier makes or hires out costumes, and a tight outfit might require holding the belly in.

clue.text: See 19
A flurry of rain gets beneath split on a riverbank

indicators.note: in a down clue, the later letters come beneath the first word

parts.note: a rip is a tear or split

indicators.note: a flurry is a confused whirl, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A sudden shower of rain falls through a gap onto a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: RAIN rearranged gives RIAN; A and RIAN go below RIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Riparian is the adjective for things relating to or situated on the banks of a river.

clue.text: Act against old PM and visibly age

parts.note: to turn on or against someone is to oppose them; turn here means to act against
Earl Grey was British Prime Minister in the 1830s

explanation.surface: Opposing a former prime minister makes you look older.
explanation.walkthrough: Earl Grey, PM 1830 to 1834, is best known for the Great Reform Act.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair losing its colour is an outward sign of getting older.

clue.text: A good part of three months and it's still warm

indicators.note: a good part means most of a word, so the opening is dropped and the larger ending kept

parts.note: September, November and December all end in the same five letters; December stands for them here

explanation.surface: Three months of the year have passed and the weather is still mild.
explanation.walkthrough: The last five letters are shared by SeptEMBER, NovEMBER and DecEMBER, making up most of each name.
explanation.definitionFit: An ember is a glowing piece of coal or wood left in a dying fire, still hot.

clue.text: Mr James returned 'mood' paint?

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the name is reversed

parts.note: Sid James was a British comic actor of the Carry On films
temper means a state of mind or mood

explanation.surface: A comic actor's bad mood comes back, perhaps from painting.
explanation.walkthrough: SID reversed gives DIS. The question mark marks the dog-disease sense being set aside for the paint sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Distemper is a water-based paint used on walls, besides being a disease of dogs.

clue.text: Gaunt-looking rogue: suave or devious?

parts.note: a cad is a dishonourable man, a rogue

indicators.note: devious means winding and indirect, so the letters wander out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A thin-faced scoundrel: is he smooth or sly?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Devious' reads as a description of the rogue, but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadaverous means corpse-like, pale and very thin.

clue.text: Criminal boss is dope? Surprise, surprise!

parts.note: dope is slang for an illegal drug
'Lord!' is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Someone reacts with mock shock on learning a crime boss is stupid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' wants to mean an idiot; here it is the narcotic.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug lord heads a criminal organisation trafficking narcotics.

clue.text: Act prematurely and clear article by Rod

parts.note: to clear an obstacle is to jump it
the is the definite article
rod is American slang for a gun

explanation.surface: Someone acts too early and vaults clear of an item beside a fishing rod.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod looks like a man's name; it is gangster slang for a pistol.
explanation.definitionFit: To jump the gun means to start too soon, from a runner leaving before the starting pistol.

clue.text: Popular painting etc — a clue: it surprisingly is hard to understand

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
art covers painting and the like

indicators.note: surprisingly hints at an unexpected outcome, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clue about popular painting turns out to be baffling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'etc' belongs with painting: art covers painting and similar crafts, so it is not part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Inarticulate speech is unclear or badly expressed, so listeners struggle to follow it.

clue.text: Practice with vehicle almost covered in concrete

indicators.note: the shortened vehicle sits inside the concrete word

parts.note: concrete means real, actual

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is left off

parts.note: a hearse is a funeral vehicle

explanation.surface: Training session with a car nearly buried in cement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concrete' wants to be the building material; it is the adjective meaning real. HEARSE without its last letter is HEARS.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice performance before the real one.

clue.text: Dead, buried in ground, after one's separated

indicators.note: the burial comes after the numeral

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

indicators.note: the word for dead goes inside the word for ground

parts.note: sod is turf, the ground
the late means the dead, the deceased

explanation.surface: A corpse is put in the earth once someone has been parted from others.
explanation.walkthrough: LATE inside SOD gives SOLATED, after I; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolated means set apart or cut off from others.

clue.text: Wretched gang gets drunk, taking lorry off

indicators.note: the drunkard's word takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard

indicators.note: off means awry, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A miserable bunch get drunk after unloading a lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like a verb; it is the noun, a drunkard.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorry lot is an informal phrase for a pitiful or disreputable group of people.

clue.text: Controversial treatment of hair, with article (hammer?) hitting your head!

parts.note: a shock of hair is a thick mass of it
the is the definite article
to rap is to hammer or knock

indicators.note: head means the first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A hairdresser's treatment involves something being banged on your head.
explanation.definitionFit: Electroconvulsive therapy, delivering electric jolts to the brain, remains a disputed psychiatric procedure.

clue.text: Stories constructed by Spiderman?

parts.note: a tangle of falsehoods is pictured as something a spider-man would spin

explanation.walkthrough: Stories here are untruths, and Spiderman suggests something spun from silk.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes an intricate network of deceits, each falsehood propping up another.

clue.text: Trial of alternative timber

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
deal is pine or fir wood

explanation.surface: A test of a different kind of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a painful experience; historically, trial by ordeal tested guilt physically.

clue.text: See 12
Labour shortly to follow this US-style party?

definitions.text: Labour shortly to follow this US-style party?

parts.words: Labour shortly to follow this US-style party?
parts.note: labour is childbirth, which comes soon after a celebration given for an expectant mother

explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' and 'party' suggest British politics; the labour is giving birth.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an American custom of a gift-giving celebration for a mother-to-be shortly before her child arrives.

clue.text: Yeats's top poem with Latin form of singing

indicators.note: top in a down clue means the first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken
an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: The best of Yeats's verse, with some Latin, makes a kind of song.
explanation.definitionFit: Yodelling is an Alpine vocal style alternating rapidly between chest voice and falsetto.

clue.text: A dog without lead is too much!

indicators.note: the lead is the first letter, so the opening letter is removed

parts.note: Rover is a traditional name for a dog

explanation.surface: A dog let off its lead is an excessive nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a dog's leash; here it is the leading letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Over can mean excessive, as in being over the limit.

clue.text: Steed forced to accept disastrous live broadcast

indicators.note: the reshuffled horse word takes in the other letters
forced means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: disastrous suggests ruin, so these letters are jumbled too

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A horse is made to take part in a calamitous live show.
explanation.walkthrough: Both anagrams are separate: one word holds the other, each shuffled by its own signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Televised means shown on television, transmitted to viewers.

clue.text: Old film star's talk that's hard to follow without a book

indicators.note: without means one letter is removed

parts.note: gabble is rapid unintelligible speech
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A veteran actor's speech is difficult to understand without a script.
explanation.definitionFit: Clark Gable was a Hollywood leading man of the 1930s, star of Gone with the Wind.

clue.text: Bird otter somehow found in hollow dell

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are placed inside
hollow means emptied of its middle letters, leaving the outer ones

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded valley

indicators.note: somehow implies an unexplained rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher spots an otter in a sunken valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hollow' looks like a description of the dell, but it means emptying the word of its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: The dotterel is a small plover; dottrel is a variant spelling of its name.

clue.text: 'All you can inhale' — final 20% off charge on coke, say, but not ecstasy

indicators.note: off means the picked letter is taken away from the charge word

parts.note: a lunge is a sudden forward charge

indicators.note: the charge word has five letters, so its final fifth is just its last letter
but not means the following letter is taken out

parts.note: coke is an example of a fuel
E is the abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: An advert for a drug-fuelled binge, minus the ecstasy, offering unlimited breathing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coke' teases the drug, but here it is a smokeless fuel made from coal; a lunge is a forward thrust in fencing.
explanation.definitionFit: A lungful is the full quantity of air the chest can take in a single breath.
